{"type_":"Posts","comments":[],"posts":[{"post":{"id":54829055,"name":"If EACv2 comes to Linux, could Widevine L1 theoretically come too?","body":"For those who don’t know, Widevine is Google's DRM system for streaming services.
L3 (used on browsers such as Chrome or Firefox, even on Linux) allows up to 1080p depending on the service, generally less. L1, currently available only on proprietary systems such as Android, allows higher resolutions. Windows works with Microsoft's PlayReady, same problem but we're never getting that.
L1 requires trusted system, just like anti cheats. Other despicable DRMs like Denuvo for video games work just fine under Proton.

Basically, not having Widevine L1 on Linux means being stuck at 720p on Netflix.
I despise DRM but I think that, just like anti-cheat software, it’s a barrier to the widespread adoption of Linux. I don't care about piracy, I do it a lot, but I don't think everyone is able to give up Netflix.

Linux is a family of open source Unix-like operating systems based on the Linux kernel, an operating system kernel first released on September 17, 1991 by Linus Torvalds. Linux is typically packaged in a Linux distribution (or distro for short).

Distributions include the Linux kernel and supporting system software and libraries, many of which are provided by the GNU Project. Many Linux distributions use the word "Linux" in their name, but the Free Software Foundation uses the name GNU/Linux to emphasize the importance of GNU software, causing some controversy.

Working elephants have long played an important role in the conservation of Nepal’s wildlife and wildlands. Their height and sharp sense of their surroundings keep researchers safe from tigers and other predators, and they’re also used on patrols. But dwindling captive elephant populations and opposition to using the highly intelligent animals as beasts of burden are changing the long-term outlook for working elephants and the men known as mahouts who work with them. Dr. Amir Sadaula works closely with elephants and mahouts as a veterinary officer at the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), which operates a biodiversity conservation center on the edge of Chitwan National Park. There, NTNC employs eight trained elephants and teams of mahouts to aid in wild animal rescue and research work. “Without [the] elephant, we could not do the rescue,” Sadaula says. Mahouts Promod Chaudhary, left, and Upendra Kachadiya enter a river for their elephants to bathe while returning from grazing in Chitwan National Park, Nepal, on May 19, 2026. Image by Henry Doellinger for Mongabay. In addition to elephants that aid researchers, privately owned elephants also walk the streets of Sauraha, a community adjacent to Chitwan.
